   814→def get_kfold_reward_response(root, db, Beh):
   815→    dat = {}
   816→    for ndb in db:
   817→        aHV = load_retino(ndb, root = os.path.join(root, 'retinotopy'))['neu_ar_idx']['aHV']
   818→        mHV = load_retino(ndb, root = os.path.join(root, 'retinotopy'))['neu_ar_idx']['mHV']
   819→        spk = load_spk(ndb, root=os.path.join(root, 'spk'))
   820→        spk = stats.zscore(spk, axis=1)
   821→        interp_spk = load_interp_spk(ndb, root=os.path.join(root, 'process_data'))
   822→        u_spk = interp_spk[:, :, 5:40].mean(2) # take mean activity within texture area, starting from 5 (0.5 meter)
   823→        spk0 = stats.zscore(interp_spk.reshape(interp_spk.shape[0], -1), axis=1).reshape(interp_spk.shape)
   824→        
   825→        if 'stimtype' in ndb.keys():
   826→            beh = Beh['%s_%s_%s_%s'%(ndb['mname'], ndb['datexp'], ndb['blk'], ndb['stimtype'])]
   827→            mname = ndb['mname'] + '_' + ndb['stimtype']
   828→        else:
   829→            beh = Beh['%s_%s_%s'%(ndb['mname'], ndb['datexp'], ndb['blk'])]
   830→            mname = ndb['mname']
   831→        SoundFr = beh['SoundFr'].astype(int)
   832→        Pos = np.mod(beh['SoundDelPos'], beh['Corridor_Length']) # reward positions and cue positions are highly correlated in reward corridor
   833→                                                                   # since non-reward corridor doesn't have reward, so we use cue positions instead
   834→        u_pos = Pos.mean()
   835→        if any(Pos<0):
   836→            print('some cue frame index are nagtive')
   837→        uniqW, WallN, isRew, ntrials = beh['UniqWalls'], beh['WallName'], beh['isRew'], beh['ntrials']
   838→        stim_id = beh['stim_id']
   839→        stim1 = WallN==uniqW[stim_id==2]
   840→        stim2 = WallN==uniqW[stim_id==0]
   841→
   842→        resp = np.empty(interp_spk.shape[1:])
   843→        stim_resp = np.empty(interp_spk.shape[1:])
   844→
   845→        ranges = np.array([15, 15])
   846→        spk2Flick = np.empty((ntrials, np.sum(ranges))) * np.nan
   847→        lick2Flick = np.empty((ntrials, np.sum(ranges))) * np.nan
   848→        Flick_pos = np.empty(ntrials) * np.nan
   849→        spk2Cue = np.empty((ntrials, np.sum(ranges))) * np.nan
   850→        lick2Cue = np.empty((ntrials, np.sum(ranges))) * np.nan
   851→        
   852→        random.seed(2025)
   853→        tr_shuf = np.random.permutation(ntrials)
   854→        nfold = 10
   855→        k_tr = int(np.ceil(beh['ntrials']/nfold))
   856→        for k in range(nfold): # 10 folds
   857→            test_tr = np.zeros(ntrials).astype(bool)
   858→            test_tr[tr_shuf[k * k_tr : (k+1) * k_tr]] = True # test trials index
   859→            ### using training trials to get dprimes
   860→            dp0 = dprime(spk[:, SoundFr[stim1 & ~test_tr]], spk[:, SoundFr[stim2 & ~test_tr]]) # equivilent to using all frames within the whole corridor
   861→            dp1 = dprime(u_spk[:, (Pos > u_pos) & stim1 & ~test_tr & isRew],

   863→            thr = np.percentile(dp1[aHV], 95) # dprime at 95 percentile in aHV

   866→            sel_spk = spk0[sel_idx, :, :][:, test_tr]

   881→        dat[mname] = {'resp':resp, 'stim_resp':stim_resp, 'beh':beh, 'resp2FL':spk2Flick, 'FL_pos':Flick_pos, 'lick2FL':lick2Flick, 'resp2Cue':spk2Cue, 'lick2Cue':lick2Cue}

   913→def spk_2_firstLick(spk, beh, ranges=[15, 15], bins=30):
   914→    """ranges: frames included before and after first lick
   915→        spk: one dimensional activity
   916→    """
   917→    lickPos, lickFr, lickTr, ntrials  = beh['LickPos'], beh['LickFr'].astype(int), beh['LickTrind'].astype(int), beh['ntrials']
   918→    spk2Flick = np.empty((ntrials, np.sum(ranges))) * np.nan
   919→    lick2Flick = np.empty((ntrials, np.sum(ranges))) * np.nan
   920→    Flick_pos = np.empty(ntrials) * np.nan
   921→    for n in range(ntrials):
   922→        idx = lickTr==n
   923→        if idx.sum()>0:
   924→            F_id = int(lickFr[np.where(idx)[0][0]]) # first lick frame index
   925→            lickFr_offset = lickFr - F_id # align lick frame to first lick
   926→            temp_spk = spk[F_id - ranges[0] : F_id+ranges[1]]
   927→            if len(temp_spk)>0:
   928→                Flick_pos[n] = lickPos[idx][0]
   929→                spk2Flick[n] = spk[F_id - ranges[0] : F_id+ranges[1]]
   930→                temp_lick = lickFr_offset[(lickFr_offset>=-ranges[0]) & (lickFr_offset<=ranges[1])] + ranges[0]
   931→                hist, edge = np.histogram(temp_lick, bins=bins, range=(0, np.sum(ranges)))
   932→                lick2Flick[n] = hist
   933→    return Flick_pos, spk2Flick, lick2Flick
   934→
   935→def spk_2_cue(spk, beh, ranges=[15, 15], bins=30):
   936→    """ranges: frames included before and after cue frame
   937→        spk: one dimensional activity
   938→    """
   939→    SoundFr, lickFr, lickTr, ntrials  = beh['SoundFr'].astype(int), beh['LickFr'].astype(int), beh['LickTrind'].astype(int), beh['ntrials']
   940→    spk2Cue = np.empty((ntrials, np.sum(ranges))) * np.nan
   941→    lick2Cue = np.empty((ntrials, np.sum(ranges))) * np.nan
   942→    for n in range(ntrials):
   943→        spk2Cue[n] = spk[SoundFr[n] - ranges[0] : SoundFr[n] + ranges[1]]
   944→        
   945→        temp_lick = lickFr[(lickFr>=SoundFr[n]-ranges[0]) & (lickFr<=SoundFr[n]+ranges[1])] - SoundFr[n] + ranges[0]
   946→        hist, edge = np.histogram(temp_lick, bins=bins, range=(0, np.sum(ranges)))
   947→        lick2Cue[n] = hist
   948→    return spk2Cue, lick2Cue

   100→def interp_value(v, vind, tind):
   101→    """v: value; vind: index; tind: target index"""
   102→    Model_ = interpolate.interp1d(vind, v, fill_value='extrapolate')
   103→    return Model_(tind)

   105→def spk_pos_interp(raw_spk=[], accum_pos=[], corridorLen=[], new_shape=[]):
   106→    """raw_spk: neurons x frames
   107→        accum_pos: accumulated position, should be increasement
   108→        corridorLen: length of corrdior
   109→        new_shape: [0]: trials number. [1]: bins for each corridor, if[1]==0 then bins=corridorLen
   110→    """
   111→    if len(new_shape)==2:
   112→        if new_shape[1]==0:
   113→            new_shape[1] = corridorLen
   114→    linPos = np.arange(0, new_shape[0], 1/new_shape[1])
   115→    spk_resh = []
   116→    for s in range(raw_spk.shape[0]): # loop through neurons
   117→        spk_resh.append(np.reshape(interp_value(raw_spk[s, :], accum_pos/corridorLen, linPos), (int(new_shape[0]), int(new_shape[1]))))
   118→    return np.array(spk_resh)

   217→def lickCount(dats, def_range=[]):
   218→    """return binary lick response for each trial"""
   219→    befRew, aftRew, inRange = [], [], []
   220→    for n in range(dats['ntrials']):
   221→        RewTime, SoundTime = dats['RewTime'], dats['SoundTime']
   222→        cue_del = SoundTime + dats['Reward_Delay_ms']/(1000*3600*24) # convert to datenum 
   223→        if dats['Reward_Mode']=='Passive':
   224→            befRew.append(find_between(dats['LickTime'],dats['Trial_start_time'][n],cue_del[n]))
   225→        elif dats['Reward_Mode']=='Active after cue':
   226→            befRew.append(find_between(dats['LickTime'],dats['Trial_start_time'][n],dats['Gray_space_time'][n]))
   227→        aftRew.append(find_between(dats['LickTime'],RewTime[n],dats['Gray_space_time'][n]))
   228→        if len(def_range)==2:
   229→            inRange.append(find_between(dats['LickPos'], def_range[0], def_range[1]) & (dats['LickTrind']==n))
   230→        else:
   231→            inRange.append([np.nan])
   232→
   233→    lickResp = {'befRew':np.array(befRew).sum(1)>0,
   234→                'aftRew':np.array(aftRew).sum(1)>0,
   235→                'inRange':np.array(inRange).sum(1)>0}    
   236→    return lickResp

   238→def lick_response(dats, trial_include=[], def_range=[]):
   239→    lickResp= lickCount(dats, def_range=def_range)
   240→    
   241→    Resp = {}
   242→    Resp['tex_name'] = dats['UniqWalls']
   243→    Resp['category'] = []
   244→    Resp['isRew'] = []
   245→    Resp['stim_id'] = dats['stim_id'] if 'stim_id' in dats else None
   246→    ntrials = dats['ntrials']
   247→    trial_include = np.array(trial_include)
   248→
   249→    kn = list(lickResp.keys())
   250→    for w,wn in enumerate(Resp['tex_name']):
   251→        Resp[wn] = {}
   252→        for k in range(len(kn)):
   253→            idx = dats['WallName']==wn
   254→            trial_n = np.arange(ntrials)
   255→            if len(trial_include)==2:
   256→                idx = idx & (trial_n>=trial_include[0]) & (trial_n<=trial_include[1])
   257→
   258→            Resp[wn][kn[k]] = np.array([np.mean(lickResp[kn[k]][idx]), 
   259→                                        np.std(lickResp[kn[k]][idx], ddof=1)/np.sqrt(idx.sum())])
   260→    return Resp

   262→def get_mean_lick_response(beh, lick_typ='befRew'):

   370→def dprime(x1, x2):
   371→    """x1,x2: neurons * frames """
   372→    u1, u2 = np.nanmean(x1, 1), np.nanmean(x2, 1)
   373→    sig1, sig2 = np.nanstd(x1, 1), np.nanstd(x2, 1)
   374→    return 2 * (u1 - u2) / (sig1 + sig2)

   376→def get_dist_img(xpos, ypos, sel_idx=None, sig=30, sig_bg=30, xoff=800, yoff=800):
   377→    from scipy import ndimage
   378→    """create an binary image for indicate neurons' position using xpos and ypos
   379→    """
   380→    x, y = xpos+xoff, ypos+yoff
   381→    bg, img = np.zeros((5000,5000)), np.zeros((5000,5000))
   382→    bg[y.astype(int), x.astype(int)] = 1.0
   383→    bg = ndimage.gaussian_filter(bg, sigma=1, truncate=sig_bg)>0 # create a background map
   384→    bg = bg.astype(float)
   385→    bg[bg==False] = np.nan # fill empty space with nan
   386→    
   387→    if any(sel_idx != None):
   388→        img[y[sel_idx].astype(int), x[sel_idx].astype(int)] = 1
   389→    img = ndimage.gaussian_filter(img, sigma=sig)
   390→    img[np.isnan(bg)] = np.nan
   391→    img = np.fliplr(img)
   392→    return img

   394→def Get_density_map(dprime, retinotopy, dp_thr=0.3, typ='both', n_down = 10):
   395→    """dp_thr: threshold,
   396→    n_down: down sample ratio"""
   397→    xoff, yoff =800,800   
   398→    img = []
   399→    for i in range(len(dprime)):   
   400→        ixy, arid = retinotopy[i]['xy_t'], retinotopy[i]['iarea']
   401→        dp = dprime[i]
   402→        if typ=='both':
   403→            idx = abs(dp) >= dp_thr
   404→        elif typ=='stim1':
   405→            idx = dp >= dp_thr
   406→        elif typ=='stim2':
   407→            idx = dp <= -dp_thr            
   408→        idx_neu = (arid!=-1) & (arid != 7) # exclude neurons from outside of visual cortex
   409→        nneu = idx_neu.sum() # total neurons
   410→        xpos, ypos = -ixy[idx_neu, 1], ixy[idx_neu, 0]
   411→
   412→        img0 = get_dist_img(xpos, ypos, idx[idx_neu], xoff=xoff, yoff=yoff)
   413→        img.append(img0/nneu) # devided by total neurons
   414→    img = np.nanmean(np.array(img), axis=0) # mean across mice
   415→    imgs = {'img':img[::n_down, ::n_down], 'n_down':n_down} # scale down
   416→    return imgs

   503→def Get_coding_direction(db, Beh, stim_ref=[2, 0], prc=5, root='', 
   504→                            load_save_interp_spk=1, interp_spk_path='', n_bef = 10):
   505→    """stim_ref = [2, 0]: 'circle1':0, 'circle2':1, 'leaf1':2, 'leaf2':3, 'leaf3':4, 'leaf1_swap1':5, 'leaf1_swap2':6'
   506→       prc: percentile
   507→       n_bef: append n_bef postion from previous trial
   508→       step1: choose neurons selective to stim_ref with percentile (prc)
   509→       step2: calculate response along coding direction of stim_ref for all stimuli 
   510→     """
   511→    all_stim = ['circle1','circle2','leaf1','leaf2','leaf3','leaf1_swap1','leaf1_swap2']
   512→    spk_proj_1, spk_proj_2 = {}, {}
   513→    for n, ndb in enumerate(db):
   514→        mname, m = ndb['mname'], 1
   515→        while mname in list(spk_proj_1.keys()):  # for a mouse has multiple sessions
   516→            mname = ndb['mname'] + '_%d'%(m)
   517→            m += 1 
   518→
   519→        spk_proj_1[mname], spk_proj_2[mname] = {}, {}
   520→
   521→        # load retinotopy 
   522→        ret = load_retino(ndb, root=os.path.join(root, 'retinotopy'))
   523→        areas = [ret['neu_ar_idx'][ky] for ky in ret['neu_ar_idx']] # get area index of neurons 
   524→        # load spks
   525→        spk = load_spk(ndb, root=os.path.join(root, 'spk'))
   526→        nneu, nfr = spk.shape         
   527→        # load behavior
   528→        kn = '%s_%s_%s'%(ndb['mname'], ndb['datexp'], ndb['blk'])
   529→        beh = Beh[kn]
   530→        ntrials, uniqW, WallN, stim_id = beh['ntrials'], beh['UniqWalls'], beh['WallName'], beh['stim_id']
   531→        CL = beh['Corridor_Length']
   532→        trInd = np.arange(ntrials)
   533→        ft_trInd = beh['ft_trInd'][:nfr]
   534→        ft_WallN = beh['ft_WallID'][:nfr]
   535→        ft_AcumPos = beh['ft_PosCum'][:nfr]
   536→        VRmove = beh['ft_move'][:nfr]>0
   537→        corr_fr = beh['ft_CorrSpc'][:nfr] & VRmove
   538→        grey_fr = beh['ft_GraySpc'][:nfr] & VRmove    
   539→
   540→        if load_save_interp_spk:
   541→            interp_spk = load_interp_spk(ndb, root=interp_spk_path)
   542→            print('load interpolated spk..')
   543→        else:
   544→            interp_spk = get_interpPos_spk(spk[:, VRmove], ft_AcumPos[VRmove], 
   545→                                                 ntrials, n_bins=60, lengths=CL)
   546→        spk_resh = interp_spk.reshape((nneu,-1))
   547→
   548→        # use odd trials to get dprime, using the raw frames activity instead of mean activity of each trial
   549→        stim1_fr = (ft_WallN == uniqW[stim_id==stim_ref[0]]) & (ft_trInd % 2 == 0) & corr_fr # odd trials frames
   550→        stim2_fr = (ft_WallN == uniqW[stim_id==stim_ref[1]]) & (ft_trInd % 2 == 0) & corr_fr # odd trials frames
   551→        grey_fr = (ft_trInd % 2==0) & grey_fr # odd trials gray frames
   552→        dp = dprime(spk[:, stim1_fr], spk[:, stim2_fr]) # get dprime 
   553→        # select neurons that response more in the texture area than in the gray space
   554→        corr_neu = (spk[:, stim1_fr].mean(1) > spk[:, grey_fr].mean(1)) | (spk[:, stim2_fr].mean(1) > spk[:, grey_fr].mean(1))
   555→
   556→        stim1_tr = WallN==uniqW[stim_id==stim_ref[0]][0] # stim1 trials
   557→        stim2_tr = WallN==uniqW[stim_id==stim_ref[1]][0] # stim2 trials
   558→
   559→        corr_spk = interp_spk[:, :, :40].copy() # get activity in the texture area 
   560→        u0 = interp_spk[:,:,42:52].reshape((nneu, -1)).mean(1, keepdims=1) # mean activity in gray space    
   561→        stim1_std = corr_spk[:, stim1_tr].reshape((nneu, -1)).std(1, keepdims=1) # std for stim1
   562→        stim2_std = corr_spk[:, stim2_tr].reshape((nneu, -1)).std(1, keepdims=1) # std for stim2    
   563→        # center to gray space, normalized by std of stim1 and stim2 
   564→        spk_norm = (2 * (spk_resh - u0) / (stim1_std + stim2_std)).reshape(interp_spk.shape)
   565→        # append activity from gray space of the previous trial 
   566→        gray_prev = np.empty((nneu, ntrials, n_bef)) * np.nan
   567→        gray_prev[:, 1:] = spk_norm[:, :-1, 60-n_bef:]
   568→        spk_norm = np.concatenate((gray_prev, spk_norm), axis=2) # concatenate the inter-trial-interval from previous trial    
   569→        print('done normalization..')
   570→        for i, iarn in enumerate(['V1','mHV','lHV','aHV']): # ['V1','mHV','lHV','aHV']
   571→            thrs = np.percentile(dp[corr_neu & areas[i]], [100-prc, prc]) # get dprime value at percentile for corridor neurons and area    
   572→            stim1_idx = (dp >= thrs[0]) & corr_neu & areas[i]
   573→            stim2_idx = (dp <= thrs[1]) & corr_neu & areas[i]    
   574→            spk_proj_1[mname][iarn] = []
   575→            spk_proj_2[mname][iarn] = []
   576→
   577→            for j in range(7): #['circle1','circle2','leaf1','leaf2','leaf3','leaf1_swap1','leaf1_swap2']
   578→                if j in stim_ref:
   579→                    # only take even trials for stimuli whhich are used for getting the dprime
   580→                    tr_idx = (WallN==uniqW[stim_id==j]) & (trInd % 2 == 1) 
   581→                else:
   582→                    if np.sum(stim_id==j) > 0: # if stimulus is presented
   583→                        tr_idx = WallN == uniqW[stim_id == j]
   584→                    else:
   585→                        tr_idx = np.zeros(len(WallN)).astype(bool) 
   586→                spk_proj_1[mname][iarn].append(spk_norm[stim1_idx][:, tr_idx].mean(0)) # mean across neurons
   587→                spk_proj_2[mname][iarn].append(spk_norm[stim2_idx][:, tr_idx].mean(0)) # mean across neurons
   588→        print(n)
   589→    all_dat ={}
   590→    all_dat['notes'] = 'coding direction of %s - %s'%(all_stim[stim_ref[0]], all_stim[stim_ref[1]])
   591→    all_dat['proj_2_stim1'] = spk_proj_1
   592→    all_dat['proj_2_stim2'] = spk_proj_2
   593→    all_dat['all_stim'] = np.array(all_stim)
   594→    all_dat['stim_ref'] = stim_ref
   595→    all_dat['pos_length'] = spk_norm.shape[2]
   596→    all_dat['pos_from_prev'] = n_bef    
   597→    return all_dat

   601→       step1: choose neurons selective to stim_ref with percentile (prc), using training trials

   913→def spk_2_firstLick(spk, beh, ranges=[15, 15], bins=30):
   914→    """ranges: frames included before and after first lick
   915→        spk: one dimensional activity
   916→    """
   917→    lickPos, lickFr, lickTr, ntrials  = beh['LickPos'], beh['LickFr'].astype(int), beh['LickTrind'].astype(int), beh['ntrials']
   918→    spk2Flick = np.empty((ntrials, np.sum(ranges))) * np.nan
   919→    lick2Flick = np.empty((ntrials, np.sum(ranges))) * np.nan
   920→    Flick_pos = np.empty(ntrials) * np.nan
   921→    for n in range(ntrials):
   922→        idx = lickTr==n
   923→        if idx.sum()>0:
   924→            F_id = int(lickFr[np.where(idx)[0][0]]) # first lick frame index
   925→            lickFr_offset = lickFr - F_id # align lick frame to first lick
   926→            temp_spk = spk[F_id - ranges[0] : F_id+ranges[1]]
   927→            if len(temp_spk)>0:
   928→                Flick_pos[n] = lickPos[idx][0]
   929→                spk2Flick[n] = spk[F_id - ranges[0] : F_id+ranges[1]]
   930→                temp_lick = lickFr_offset[(lickFr_offset>=-ranges[0]) & (lickFr_offset<=ranges[1])] + ranges[0]
   931→                hist, edge = np.histogram(temp_lick, bins=bins, range=(0, np.sum(ranges)))
   932→                lick2Flick[n] = hist
   933→    return Flick_pos, spk2Flick, lick2Flick
   934→
   935→def spk_2_cue(spk, beh, ranges=[15, 15], bins=30):
   936→    """ranges: frames included before and after cue frame
   937→        spk: one dimensional activity
   938→    """
   939→    SoundFr, lickFr, lickTr, ntrials  = beh['SoundFr'].astype(int), beh['LickFr'].astype(int), beh['LickTrind'].astype(int), beh['ntrials']
   940→    spk2Cue = np.empty((ntrials, np.sum(ranges))) * np.nan
   941→    lick2Cue = np.empty((ntrials, np.sum(ranges))) * np.nan
   942→    for n in range(ntrials):
   943→        spk2Cue[n] = spk[SoundFr[n] - ranges[0] : SoundFr[n] + ranges[1]]
   944→        
   945→        temp_lick = lickFr[(lickFr>=SoundFr[n]-ranges[0]) & (lickFr<=SoundFr[n]+ranges[1])] - SoundFr[n] + ranges[0]
   946→        hist, edge = np.histogram(temp_lick, bins=bins, range=(0, np.sum(ranges)))
   947→        lick2Cue[n] = hist
   948→    return spk2Cue, lick2Cue

import numpy as np

# Check the paper for frame rate and corridor details
# From methods.txt: fs = 3.17Hz, corridor 4m long, 2m gray space, VR constant speed 60cm/s
# Corridor_Length = 60 (decimeters = 6 meters total?), Texture_Length = 40 (4m), Gray_Space_length = 20 (2m) 
# So positions are in decimeters

# Let's understand the temporal structure better
beh = np.load('data/beh/Beh_sup_test1.npy', allow_pickle=1).item()
dat = beh['TX60_2021_06_07_1']

# Frame rate
ft = dat['ft']
dt = np.diff(ft) * 24 * 3600  # convert from datenum to seconds
print(f'Mean frame interval: {np.nanmean(dt):.4f} s')
print(f'Frame rate: {1/np.nanmean(dt):.2f} Hz')

# Trial structure
print(f'ntrials: {dat[\"ntrials\"]}')
startfr = dat['StartFr']
grayfr = dat['GrayFr']
endfr = dat['EndFr']

print(f'Mean gray frames: {np.nanmean(endfr - grayfr):.1f}')
print(f'Mean total trial frames: {np.nanmean(endfr - startfr):.1f}')

# But since VR moves at constant speed when running, time in corridor is fixed
# 4m corridor at 0.6 m/s = 6.67 seconds
# At 3.17 Hz, that's about 21 frames
print(f'Expected corridor frames at 60cm/s, 4m: {4/0.6 * 3.17:.1f}')
print(f'Expected gray frames at 60cm/s, 2m: {2/0.6 * 3.17:.1f}')

import numpy as np

# Check the paper for frame rate and corridor details
# From methods.txt: fs = 3.17Hz, corridor 4m long, 2m gray space, VR constant speed 60cm/s

steps.reasoning_content:
Let me understand the task better. The paper describes mice running through virtual corridors with visual stimuli. The neural data is calcium imaging (deconvolved fluorescence). I need to create a decoder dataset.

Key decisions:
1. What constitutes a "session"? Each recording session (unique mname_datexp_blk combination)
2. What constitutes a "trial"? Each corridor traversal
3. Neural data: deconvolved spikes, shape (n_neurons, n_timepoints) per trial
4. Temporal alignment: trial start (corridor entry) as specified
5. Time bin size: ~315 ms (1/3.17 Hz)
6. Corridor structure: 60 bins total with 40 bins of texture and 20 bins of gray space

For the decoder, I'm setting up inputs like time to sound cue, training day, elapsed time in trial, and reward availability, with outputs for visual stimulus type, licking behavior, position discretized into 4 bins, and running speed also in 4 bins. I need to figure out whether each trial spans just the corridor or includes the gray space section as well.

The reference code distinguishes between corridor and gray space frames, and identifies movement periods when the mouse is actively running above a speed threshold. Since the paper focuses only on running periods for analysis, I should probably include all frames within a trial but be mindful that trial length varies depending on when the mouse stops to collect rewards. The trials are aligned to corridor entry, and since the VR moves at constant speed when running, I need to handle the variable frame counts by using spatial binning rather than time-based binning. be consistent across trials. So I should use spatial binning with the position-interpolated neural data, which naturally gives me time bins of roughly 167 ms when the mouse is actively running. So the measured frame counts don't quite match the theoretical calculation, likely because the VR system has periods of inactivity when the mouse input slows down. Rather than trying to reconcile the frame timing discrepancies, I'll follow the reference approach and represent each trial as 60 spatial bins dividing the corridor and gray space regions.

Since the VR moves at a constant 6 dm/s and each spatial bin spans 1 dm, that means each bin corresponds to roughly 167 milliseconds of time. This gives me a consistent temporal resolution for the decoder across all trials.

Now I'm thinking through the decoder inputs and outputs. The key input is time to sound cue—for each position in the corridor, I need to calculate how much time remains until the sound plays. Since the sound position is somewhere in the 0-40 range (the texture area), I can compute this as (SoundPos - current_position) divided by the VR speed. Let me figure out exactly which position variable to use for the sound cue location. For day of training, I need to figure out what "continuous, time-varying" means in this context. It seems like it should be constant within a trial and session since all trials on the same day share that value, but it varies across different sessions. I'll treat it as a constant value across all time bins within a trial.

Now moving to time since trial start, which should increase continuously from the beginning of each trial.

For reward availability, I'm checking whether the animal is in a rewarded corridor using the behavioral data.

For the decoder outputs, I need to extract the visual stimulus category from the wall names, map licking events to individual time bins, and discretize the corridor position into four 1-meter spatial bins.

Now I'm working through how to handle the spatial binning—the texture corridor is 4 meters long, so four equal bins of 1 meter each makes sense: [0-1m), [1-2m), [2-3m), [3-4m). The gray space beyond that isn't part of the corridor proper, so I'll focus on just the texture area. I'll include all 60 spatial bins with position categories 0-3 for the corridor and category 4 for gray space. For running speed, I need to compute quantiles from the actual data to create 4 equal-frequency bins. Now I'm planning the full pipeline: load all sessions, extract behavior and neural data, assign brain regions using retinotopy, and interpolate the neural activity into spatial bins across trials.

I need to handle session deduplication carefully since some recordings appear across multiple experiment types with different stimulus subsets—each neural data file is uniquely identified by the mouse name, date, and block number. I need to check which sessions appear across different experiment types to understand how the behavior data maps to the recordings.

steps.reasoning_content:
Good - the behavior data is duplicated across experiment types. The same session has the same behavior data regardless of which experiment type it's listed under. The experiment types just categorize sessions differently for analysis purposes. So I can safely use any one of the behavior files that contains a given session.

Now let me plan the conversion approach:

1. Each unique recording session (89 total) = one session in the decoder dataset
2. For each session, load the behavior from whichever experiment type contains it
3. Load neural data, concatenate planes
4. Load retinotopy for brain region assignment
5. Interpolate neural data into spatial bins (60 bins per trial)
6. Build inputs and outputs for each trial

I need to think about neuron filtering. The reference code uses area assignments to categorize neurons into V1 and different higher visual areas based on their iarea values. Neurons with iarea == -1 or iarea == 7 are excluded since they're outside visual cortex. For the decoder, I should include all neurons that have valid brain region assignments rather than restricting to specific areas.

The reference code also only uses frames when the VR is actively moving (ft_move > 0), which aligns with the paper's focus on running periods. I'll organize brain regions as V1, mHV, lHV, and aHV following the reference implementation.

For the temporal structure, each trial has 60 spatial bins when interpolated, with a time bin size of about 166.67 milliseconds based on the 6 dm/s speed and 1 dm bin size.

Now I'm mapping out the inputs and outputs: the first 40 bins represent the texture corridor while the last 20 are gray space. For inputs, I need to calculate time to the sound cue based on position, extract the training day from experiment info, compute elapsed time from trial start, and track reward availability. For outputs, I'm extracting the visual stimulus category from wall names, mapping lick positions to spatial bins using lick timing data, and binning position into corridor segments.

I'm also thinking through how to handle the "day of training" field more carefully—some sessions have an explicit 'days' field while others only have 'sess#', so I should prioritize the 'days' field when available and compute the day number from session information when it's not.

For sessions without explicit day information, I'll calculate the day relative to each mouse's first session by parsing the dates from the datexp field. I should also verify that all 89 sessions meet the requirement of having at least two trials, and check the neuron counts to understand the data scale better. Now I'm ready to start writing the conversion script since I have a solid grasp of the data structure.

For handling the stimtype field that appears in some experiment types, I need to decide how to map sessions to experiment types. Since each session is a unique recording with the same underlying behavior data regardless of experiment type, I'll use the first experiment type encountered for each session to avoid duplicates. The stim_id might vary across experiment types since they analyze different stimulus subsets, but the raw behavior data like WallName and LickPos should remain consistent for the same session.

--- Page 9 ---
Methods
All experimental procedures were conducted according to the Institu-
tional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC), and received ethical 
approval from the IACUC board at the HHMI Janelia Research Campus.
Experimental methods
Animals. We performed 89 recordings in 19 mice bred to express 
GCaMP6s in excitatory neurons: TetO-GCaMP6s × camK2a-tTa mice 
(available as RRID:IMSR_JAX:024742 and RRID:IMSR_JAX:003010)52. 
Of these mice, 13 were male and 6 were female, and ranged from 2 to 11 
months of age. Mice were housed in reverse light cycle, and were pair 
housed with their siblings before and after surgery. The mice had a run-
ning wheel in their cage, as well as corncob bedding with Nestlets. Dur-

Methods
All experimental procedures were conducted according to the Institu-
tional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC), and received ethical 
approval from the IACUC board at the HHMI Janelia Research Campus.
Experimental methods
Animals. We performed 89 recordings in 19 mice bred to express 
GCaMP6s in excitatory neurons: TetO-GCaMP6s × camK2a-tTa mice 
(available as RRID:IMSR_JAX:024742 and RRID:IMSR_JAX:003010)52. 
Of these mice, 13 were male and 6 were female, and ranged from 2 to 11 
months of age. Mice were housed in reverse light cycle, and were pair 
housed with their siblings before and after surgery. The mice had a run-
ning wheel in their cage, as well as corncob bedding with Nestlets. Dur-
ing training and imaging periods, we replaced the running wheel with 
a tube, to potentially motivate the mice to run longer while head fixed. 
Owing to the stability of the cranial window surgery, we often used the 
same mice for multiple experiments in the laboratory: two of the mice 
were used in ref. 53. Two of the mice were raised in complete darkness. 
We did not see differences compared with normal-reared mice, so we 
pooled them together. It was not possible to blind the experimenter 
with respect to behavioural experiments that involved water depri-
vation (see below). The number of mice in each experimental group 
was chosen to be comparable with other studies involving complex 
behaviour and imaging procedures such as ours. Mice were randomly 
assigned into groups where relevant.
We also used 23 C57 female mice for behaviour-only experiments. 
These mice were only implanted with a headbar and not a cranial win-
dow.
Surgical procedures. Surgeries were performed in adult mice (post-
natal day 35 (P35)–P333) following procedures previously described54. 
In brief, mice were anaesthetized with isoflurane while a craniotomy 
was performed. Marcaine (no more than 8 mg kg−1) was injected subcu-
taneously beneath the incision area, and warmed fluids + 5% dextrose 
and 0.1 mg kg−1 buprenorphine (systemic analgesic) were administered 
subcutaneously along with 2 mg kg−1 dexamethasone via the intramus-
cular route. For mice with cranial windows, measurements were taken to 
determine bregma-lambda distance and the location of a 4-mm circular 
window over the V1 cortex, as far lateral and caudal as possible without 
compromising the stability of the implant. A 4 + 5-mm double window 
was placed into the craniotomy so that the 4-mm window replaced the 
previously removed bone piece and the 5-mm window lay over the 
edge of the bone. After surgery, 5 mg kg−1 ketoprofen was administered 
subcutaneously and the mice were allowed to recover on heat. The 
mice were monitored for pain or distress, and 5 mg kg−1 ketoprofen 
was administered for 2 days following surgery.
Imaging acquisition. We used a custom-built two-photon mesoscope31 
to record neural activity, and ScanImage55 for data acquisition. We used 
a custom online z-correction module (now in ScanImage), to correct for 
z and xy drift online during the recording. As previously described54, we 
used an upgrade of the mesoscope that allowed us to approximately 
double the number of recorded neurons using temporal multiplexing56.
The mice were free to run on an air-floating ball. Mice were acclima-
tized to running on the ball for several sessions before training and 
imaging.
Visual stimuli. We showed virtual reality corridors to the mice on three 
perpendicular LED tablet screens, which surrounded each mouse 
(covering 270° of their visual field of view). To present the stimuli, we 
used PsychToolbox-3 in MATLAB57. The virtual reality corridors were 
each 4 m long, with 2 m of grey space between corridors. The corridors 
were shown in a random order. The mice moved forward in the virtual 
reality corridors by running faster than a threshold of 6 cm s−1, but the 
virtual corridors always moved at a constant speed (60 cm s−1) as long 
as mice kept running faster than the threshold. Running was detected 
using an optical tracking sensor placed close to the ball.
The virtual reality corridors were created by concatenating four 
random crops from one of four large texture images: circle, leaf, rock 
and brick (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Grating stimuli (with angles of 0° 
and 45°) were also used to create the virtual reality corridors for a subset 
of mice (‘unsupervised gratings’ and VRg mice).
For behaviour-only experiments, each mouse was trained with 
rewards on one random pair of stimuli, such as leaf–circle or rock–brick. 
Mice with unsupervised pretraining (VRn mice) were pretrained on the 
same pair on which they were trained with rewards.
For imaging experiments, mice from both the task and the unsuper-
vised cohorts were only trained on or exposed to one pair of stimuli, 
such as leaf–circle or rock–brick. For the mice exposed to the grating 
stimuli, we presented more than one pair of naturalistic stimuli before 
and after exposure to the gratings stimuli and recorded the neural 
responses to the naturalistic stimuli pairs, so each mouse can have more 
than one imaging session before and after. We also presented more than 
one pair of naturalistic stimuli to the naive mice, so each naive mouse 
can have more than one imaging session for testing naive responses.
The two different types of leaf1-swap stimuli (Extended Data Figs. 6f 
and 7a) were introduced separately for task mice but are pooled 
together for statistics analysis. The two leaf1-swap stimuli were intro-
duced in the same session for unsupervised and naive mice, but were 
treated as two different data points and pooled together for statistical 
analyses.
Water restriction procedure. Water restriction procedures were con-
ducted according to the IACUC. During the virtual reality + reward 
training condition, animals received an average of 1 ml water per day 
(range of 0.8–1.2 ml depending on health status and behavioural per-
formance). Before reaching 1 ml water per day after the initiation of 
the restriction procedure, we gradually reduced the water amount 
from 2 ml per day to 1.5 ml per day until finally to 1 ml per day. The 
behaviour-only mice were water restricted for 5 days right before 
the virtual reality + reward training condition. Once the mice finished 
the virtual reality + reward training session, the remaining water 
(0.8–1.2 ml minus the amount received during experiment) was pro-
vided 0.5 h after the training. During the whole water restriction period, 
the body weight, appearance and behaviours were monitored using a 
standard quantitative health assessment system58.
Water reward delivery and lick detection. A capacitance detector 
was connected with the metal lick port to detect licking. Mice received 
a drop of water (2.5 µl) if they correctly licked inside the reward corri-
dor. In day 1 of the virtual reality + reward training session, we always 
delivered the water passively (passive mode) so that the mice could 
get used to acquiring reward when stimuli were present. For all the 
behaviour-only mice (Fig. 5) and some of the imaging mice (Figs. 1–4), 
we switched to active-reward mode after day 1 so that the mice had to 
lick within the reward zone to trigger the water delivery. For some of 
the imaging mice (Figs. 1–4), we kept using the passive mode but added 
a delay (1 s or 1.5 s) between the sound cue and reward delivery. Given 
that mice started licking as soon as they entered the corridor and until 
they received the water, adding a delay versus active-reward mode did 
not change how the mice behaved (Figs. 1–4).
Behavioural training. All animals were handled via refined handling 
techniques for at least 3 days before being acclimated to head fixation 
on the ball. Animals were acclimated gradually (0.5–1 h per day) on the 
ball over at least 3 days until they could be head fixed without exhibiting 
any signs of distress. Then, animals began a running training regiment 
(1 h per day), which lasted for at least 5 days to ensure they could run 
smoothly and continuously on the ball before being exposed to the

closed-loop virtual linear corridor. For water-restricted mice, we trained 
them for 2 days to get used to acquiring water from the spout when no 
stimulus was presented, before the virtual reality + reward training ses-
sion. The VRn and VRg pretraining groups of mice (Fig. 5) were trained 
to acquire water from the spout on the last 2 days of unsupervised 
pretraining with no stimuli presented, after the virtual reality session 
ended to avoid the associative learning between stimuli and rewards. 
For the group without pretraining (Fig. 5), learning to get reward from 
the spout was similarly carried out after the running training session 
on the last 2 days of running training.
For the behaviour-only experiment, all animals started training in 
the virtual reality + reward training session on a Monday and continued 
training for exactly 5 days. The first day of training consisted of pas-
sive reward training, during which the reward was always delivered 
to the mouse in the rewarded corridor at the beginning of the reward 
zone. The next 4 days consisted of active reward training, during which 
the mice were required to lick in the reward zone to trigger the reward. 
This ensured a consistent training schedule during the critical learning 
period. The beginning of the reward zone was randomly chosen per 
trial from a uniform distribution between 2 m and 3 m, and continued 
until the end of the corridor. This meant that the earliest position in 
the rewarded corridor in which the mouse can receive the reward was 
a range of 2–3 m.
For imaging mice, the sound cue was presented in all trial types, for 
task and unsupervised mice, and the time of the sound cue was ran-
domly chosen per trial from a uniform distribution between positions 
0.5 m and 3.5 m. For task mice, the sound cue indicated the beginning 
of the reward zone in the rewarded corridor. The reward was delivered 
if a lick was detected after the sound cue in the rewarded corridor. As 
mice kept licking (anticipatory licking) as soon as they entered the 
reward corridors and learned to lick right after the sound cue, the 
reward delivery locations were also approximately uniformly distrib-
uted between 0.5 m and 3.5 m (Fig. 1c). In some mice, the reward was 
delivered passively with a delay after the sound cue, but these mice still 
showed anticipatory licking before the sound cue. To rule out whether 
the licking was due to detecting signals related to the reward delivery, 
such as water coming out the spout or sound produced by solenoid 
valve, we considered a lick response if the mouse licked at least once 
inside the corridor but before the sound cue. Although the rewards 
were absent, the sound cue was still presented in the unsupervised 
training experiment for consistency.
Data analysis
For analysis, we used Python 3 (ref. 59), primarily based on numpy and 
scikit-learn60,61, as well as Rastermap39. The figures were made using 
matplotlib and jupyter-notebook62,63.
Processing of calcium imaging data. Calcium imaging data were 
processed using Suite2p32, available on GitHub (www.github.com/
MouseLand/suite2p). Suite2p performs motion correction, region of 
interest detection, cell classification, neuropil correction and spike 
deconvolution as previously described64. For non-negative deconvo-
lution, we used a timescale of decay of 0.75 s (ref. 65). All our analyses 
were based on deconvolved fluorescence traces.

Methods
All experimental procedures were conducted according to the Institu-
tional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC), and received ethical 
approval from the IACUC board at the HHMI Janelia Research Campus.
Experimental methods
Animals. We performed 89 recordings in 19 mice bred to express 
GCaMP6s in excitatory neurons: TetO-GCaMP6s × camK2a-tTa mice 
(available as RRID:IMSR_JAX:024742 and RRID:IMSR_JAX:003010)52. 
Of these mice, 13 were male and 6 were female, and ranged from 2 to 11 
months of age. Mice were housed in reverse light cycle, and were pair 
housed with their siblings before and after surgery. The mice had a run-
ning wheel in their cage, as well as corncob bedding with Nestlets. Dur-
ing training and imaging periods, we replaced the running wheel with 
a tube, to potentially motivate the mice to run longer while head fixed. 
Owing to the stability of the cranial window surgery, we often used the 
same mice for multiple experiments in the laboratory: two of the mice 
were used in ref. 53. Two of the mice were raised in complete darkness. 
We did not see differences compared with normal-reared mice, so we 
pooled them together. It was not possible to blind the experimenter 
with respect to behavioural experiments that involved water depri-
vation (see below). The number of mice in each experimental group 
was chosen to be comparable with other studies involving complex 
behaviour and imaging procedures such as ours. Mice were randomly 
assigned into groups where relevant.
We also used 23 C57 female mice for behaviour-only experiments. 
These mice were only implanted with a headbar and not a cranial win-
dow.
Surgical procedures. Surgeries were performed in adult mice (post-
natal day 35 (P35)–P333) following procedures previously described54. 
In brief, mice were anaesthetized with isoflurane while a craniotomy 
was performed. Marcaine (no more than 8 mg kg−1) was injected subcu-
taneously beneath the incision area, and warmed fluids + 5% dextrose 
and 0.1 mg kg−1 buprenorphine (systemic analgesic) were administered 
subcutaneously along with 2 mg kg−1 dexamethasone via the intramus-
cular route. For mice with cranial windows, measurements were taken to 
determine bregma-lambda distance and the location of a 4-mm circular 
window over the V1 cortex, as far lateral and caudal as possible without 
compromising the stability of the implant. A 4 + 5-mm double window 
was placed into the craniotomy so that the 4-mm window replaced the 
previously removed bone piece and the 5-mm window lay over the 
edge of the bone. After surgery, 5 mg kg−1 ketoprofen was administered 
subcutaneously and the mice were allowed to recover on heat. The 
mice were monitored for pain or distress, and 5 mg kg−1 ketoprofen 
was administered for 2 days following surgery.
Imaging acquisition. We used a custom-built two-photon mesoscope31 
to record neural activity, and ScanImage55 for data acquisition. We used 
a custom online z-correction module (now in ScanImage), to correct for 
z and xy drift online during the recording. As previously described54, we 
used an upgrade of the mesoscope that allowed us to approximately 
double the number of recorded neurons using temporal multiplexing56.
The mice were free to run on an air-floating ball. Mice were acclima-
tized to running on the ball for several sessions before training and 
imaging.
Visual stimuli. We showed virtual reality corridors to the mice on three 
perpendicular LED tablet screens, which surrounded each mouse 
(covering 270° of their visual field of view). To present the stimuli, we 
used PsychToolbox-3 in MATLAB57. The virtual reality corridors were 
each 4 m long, with 2 m of grey space between corridors. The corridors 
were shown in a random order. The mice moved forward in the virtual 
reality corridors by running faster than a threshold of 6 cm s−1, but the 
virtual corridors always moved at a constant speed (60 cm s−1) as long 
as mice kept running faster than the threshold. Running was detected 
using an optical tracking sensor placed close to the ball.
The virtual reality corridors were created by concatenating four 
random crops from one of four large texture images: circle, leaf, rock 
and brick (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Grating stimuli (with angles of 0° 
and 45°) were also used to create the virtual reality corridors for a subset 
of mice (‘unsupervised gratings’ and VRg mice).
For behaviour-only experiments, each mouse was trained with 
rewards on one random pair of stimuli, such as leaf–circle or rock–brick. 
Mice with unsupervised pretraining (VRn mice) were pretrained on the 
same pair on which they were trained with rewards.
For imaging experiments, mice from both the task and the unsuper-
vised cohorts were only trained on or exposed to one pair of stimuli, 
such as leaf–circle or rock–brick. For the mice exposed to the grating 
stimuli, we presented more than one pair of naturalistic stimuli before 
and after exposure to the gratings stimuli and recorded the neural 
responses to the naturalistic stimuli pairs, so each mouse can have more 
than one imaging session before and after. We also presented more than 
one pair of naturalistic stimuli to the naive mice, so each naive mouse 
can have more than one imaging session for testing naive responses.
The two different types of leaf1-swap stimuli (Extended Data Figs. 6f 
and 7a) were introduced separately for task mice but are pooled 
together for statistics analysis. The two leaf1-swap stimuli were intro-
duced in the same session for unsupervised and naive mice, but were 
treated as two different data points and pooled together for statistical 
analyses.
Water restriction procedure. Water restriction procedures were con-
ducted according to the IACUC. During the virtual reality + reward 
training condition, animals received an average of 1 ml water per day 
(range of 0.8–1.2 ml depending on health status and behavioural per-
formance). Before reaching 1 ml water per day after the initiation of 
the restriction procedure, we gradually reduced the water amount 
from 2 ml per day to 1.5 ml per day until finally to 1 ml per day. The 
behaviour-only mice were water restricted for 5 days right before 
the virtual reality + reward training condition. Once the mice finished 
the virtual reality + reward training session, the remaining water 
(0.8–1.2 ml minus the amount received during experiment) was pro-
vided 0.5 h after the training. During the whole water restriction period, 
the body weight, appearance and behaviours were monitored using a 
standard quantitative health assessment system58.
Water reward delivery and lick detection. A capacitance detector 
was connected with the metal lick port to detect licking. Mice received 
a drop of water (2.5 µl) if they correctly licked inside the reward corri-
dor. In day 1 of the virtual reality + reward training session, we always 
delivered the water passively (passive mode) so that the mice could 
get used to acquiring reward when stimuli were present. For all the 
behaviour-only mice (Fig. 5) and some of the imaging mice (Figs. 1–4), 
we switched to active-reward mode after day 1 so that the mice had to 
lick within the reward zone to trigger the water delivery. For some of 
the imaging mice (Figs. 1–4), we kept using the passive mode but added 
a delay (1 s or 1.5 s) between the sound cue and reward delivery. Given 
that mice started licking as soon as they entered the corridor and until 
they received the water, adding a delay versus active-reward mode did 
not change how the mice behaved (Figs. 1–4).
Behavioural training. All animals were handled via refined handling 
techniques for at least 3 days before being acclimated to head fixation 
on the ball. Animals were acclimated gradually (0.5–1 h per day) on the 
ball over at least 3 days until they could be head fixed without exhibiting 
any signs of distress. Then, animals began a running training regiment 
(1 h per day), which lasted for at least 5 days to ensure they could run 
smoothly and continuously on the ball before being exposed to the 


--- Page 10 ---
Article
closed-loop virtual linear corridor. For water-restricted mice, we trained 
them for 2 days to get used to acquiring water from the spout when no 
stimulus was presented, before the virtual reality + reward training ses-
sion. The VRn and VRg pretraining groups of mice (Fig. 5) were trained 
to acquire water from the spout on the last 2 days of unsupervised 
pretraining with no stimuli presented, after the virtual reality session 
ended to avoid the associative learning between stimuli and rewards. 
For the group without pretraining (Fig. 5), learning to get reward from 
the spout was similarly carried out after the running training session 
on the last 2 days of running training.
For the behaviour-only experiment, all animals started training in 
the virtual reality + reward training session on a Monday and continued 
training for exactly 5 days. The first day of training consisted of pas-
sive reward training, during which the reward was always delivered 
to the mouse in the rewarded corridor at the beginning of the reward 
zone. The next 4 days consisted of active reward training, during which 
the mice were required to lick in the reward zone to trigger the reward. 
This ensured a consistent training schedule during the critical learning 
period. The beginning of the reward zone was randomly chosen per 
trial from a uniform distribution between 2 m and 3 m, and continued 
until the end of the corridor. This meant that the earliest position in 
the rewarded corridor in which the mouse can receive the reward was 
a range of 2–3 m.
For imaging mice, the sound cue was presented in all trial types, for 
task and unsupervised mice, and the time of the sound cue was ran-
domly chosen per trial from a uniform distribution between positions 
0.5 m and 3.5 m. For task mice, the sound cue indicated the beginning 
of the reward zone in the rewarded corridor. The reward was delivered 
if a lick was detected after the sound cue in the rewarded corridor. As 
mice kept licking (anticipatory licking) as soon as they entered the 
reward corridors and learned to lick right after the sound cue, the 
reward delivery locations were also approximately uniformly distrib-
uted between 0.5 m and 3.5 m (Fig. 1c). In some mice, the reward was 
delivered passively with a delay after the sound cue, but these mice still 
showed anticipatory licking before the sound cue. To rule out whether 
the licking was due to detecting signals related to the reward delivery, 
such as water coming out the spout or sound produced by solenoid 
valve, we considered a lick response if the mouse licked at least once 
inside the corridor but before the sound cue. Although the rewards 
were absent, the sound cue was still presented in the unsupervised 
training experiment for consistency.
Data analysis
For analysis, we used Python 3 (ref. 59), primarily based on numpy and 
scikit-learn60,61, as well as Rastermap39. The figures were made using 
matplotlib and jupyter-notebook62,63.
Processing of calcium imaging data. Calcium imaging data were 
processed using Suite2p32, available on GitHub (www.github.com/
MouseLand/suite2p). Suite2p performs motion correction, region of 
interest detection, cell classification, neuropil correction and spike 
deconvolution as previously described64. For non-negative deconvo-
lution, we used a timescale of decay of 0.75 s (ref. 65). All our analyses 
were based on deconvolved fluorescence traces.

arousal levels of the mice. Note that these data points are computed 
from original estimated deconvolved traces without interpolation.

--- Page 9 ---
Methods
All experimental procedures were conducted according to the Institu-
tional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC), and received ethical 
approval from the IACUC board at the HHMI Janelia Research Campus.
Experimental methods
Animals. We performed 89 recordings in 19 mice bred to express 
GCaMP6s in excitatory neurons: TetO-GCaMP6s × camK2a-tTa mice 
(available as RRID:IMSR_JAX:024742 and RRID:IMSR_JAX:003010)52. 
Of these mice, 13 were male and 6 were female, and ranged from 2 to 11 
months of age. Mice were housed in reverse light cycle, and were pair 
housed with their siblings before and after surgery. The mice had a run-
ning wheel in their cage, as well as corncob bedding with Nestlets. Dur-
ing training and imaging periods, we replaced the running wheel with 
a tube, to potentially motivate the mice to run longer while head fixed. 
Owing to the stability of the cranial window surgery, we often used the 
same mice for multiple experiments in the laboratory: two of the mice 
were used in ref. 53. Two of the mice were raised in complete darkness. 
We did not see differences compared with normal-reared mice, so we 
pooled them together. It was not possible to blind the experimenter 
with respect to behavioural experiments that involved water depri-
vation (see below). The number of mice in each experimental group 
was chosen to be comparable with other studies involving complex 
behaviour and imaging procedures such as ours. Mice were randomly 
assigned into groups where relevant.
We also used 23 C57 female mice for behaviour-only experiments. 
These mice were only implanted with a headbar and not a cranial win-
dow.
Surgical procedures. Surgeries were performed in adult mice (post-
natal day 35 (P35)–P333) following procedures previously described54. 
In brief, mice were anaesthetized with isoflurane while a craniotomy 
was performed. Marcaine (no more than 8 mg kg−1) was injected subcu-
taneously beneath the incision area, and warmed fluids + 5% dextrose 
and 0.1 mg kg−1 buprenorphine (systemic analgesic) were administered 
subcutaneously along with 2 mg kg−1 dexamethasone via the intramus-
cular route. For mice with cranial windows, measurements were taken to 
determine bregma-lambda distance and the location of a 4-mm circular 
window over the V1 cortex, as far lateral and caudal as possible without 
compromising the stability of the implant. A 4 + 5-mm double window 
was placed into the craniotomy so that the 4-mm window replaced the 
previously removed bone piece and the 5-mm window lay over the 
edge of the bone. After surgery, 5 mg kg−1 ketoprofen was administered 
subcutaneously and the mice were allowed to recover on heat. The 
mice were monitored for pain or distress, and 5 mg kg−1 ketoprofen 
was administered for 2 days following surgery.
Imaging acquisition. We used a custom-built two-photon mesoscope31 
to record neural activity, and ScanImage55 for data acquisition. We used 
a custom online z-correction module (now in ScanImage), to correct for 
z and xy drift online during the recording. As previously described54, we 
used an upgrade of the mesoscope that allowed us to approximately 
double the number of recorded neurons using temporal multiplexing56.
The mice were free to run on an air-floating ball. Mice were acclima-
tized to running on the ball for several sessions before training and 
imaging.
Visual stimuli. We showed virtual reality corridors to the mice on three 
perpendicular LED tablet screens, which surrounded each mouse 
(covering 270° of their visual field of view). To present the stimuli, we 
used PsychToolbox-3 in MATLAB57. The virtual reality corridors were 
each 4 m long, with 2 m of grey space between corridors. The corridors 
were shown in a random order. The mice moved forward in the virtual 
reality corridors by running faster than a threshold of 6 cm s−1, but the 
virtual corridors always moved at a constant speed (60 cm s−1) as long 
as mice kept running faster than the threshold. Running was detected 
using an optical tracking sensor placed close to the ball.
The virtual reality corridors were created by concatenating four 
random crops from one of four large texture images: circle, leaf, rock 
and brick (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Grating stimuli (with angles of 0° 
and 45°) were also used to create the virtual reality corridors for a subset 
of mice (‘unsupervised gratings’ and VRg mice).
For behaviour-only experiments, each mouse was trained with 
rewards on one random pair of stimuli, such as leaf–circle or rock–brick. 
Mice with unsupervised pretraining (VRn mice) were pretrained on the 
same pair on which they were trained with rewards.
For imaging experiments, mice from both the task and the unsuper-
vised cohorts were only trained on or exposed to one pair of stimuli, 
such as leaf–circle or rock–brick. For the mice exposed to the grating 
stimuli, we presented more than one pair of naturalistic stimuli before 
and after exposure to the gratings stimuli and recorded the neural 
responses to the naturalistic stimuli pairs, so each mouse can have more 
than one imaging session before and after. We also presented more than 
one pair of naturalistic stimuli to the naive mice, so each naive mouse 
can have more than one imaging session for testing naive responses.
The two different types of leaf1-swap stimuli (Extended Data Figs. 6f 
and 7a) were introduced separately for task mice but are pooled 
together for statistics analysis. The two leaf1-swap stimuli were intro-
duced in the same session for unsupervised and naive mice, but were 
treated as two different data points and pooled together for statistical 
analyses.
Water restriction procedure. Water restriction procedures were con-
ducted according to the IACUC. During the virtual reality + reward 
training condition, animals received an average of 1 ml water per day 
(range of 0.8–1.2 ml depending on health status and behavioural per-
formance). Before reaching 1 ml water per day after the initiation of 
the restriction procedure, we gradually reduced the water amount 
from 2 ml per day to 1.5 ml per day until finally to 1 ml per day. The 
behaviour-only mice were water restricted for 5 days right before 
the virtual reality + reward training condition. Once the mice finished 
the virtual reality + reward training session, the remaining water 
(0.8–1.2 ml minus the amount received during experiment) was pro-
vided 0.5 h after the training. During the whole water restriction period, 
the body weight, appearance and behaviours were monitored using a 
standard quantitative health assessment system58.
Water reward delivery and lick detection. A capacitance detector 
was connected with the metal lick port to detect licking. Mice received 
a drop of water (2.5 µl) if they correctly licked inside the reward corri-
dor. In day 1 of the virtual reality + reward training session, we always 
delivered the water passively (passive mode) so that the mice could 
get used to acquiring reward when stimuli were present. For all the 
behaviour-only mice (Fig. 5) and some of the imaging mice (Figs. 1–4), 
we switched to active-reward mode after day 1 so that the mice had to 
lick within the reward zone to trigger the water delivery. For some of 
the imaging mice (Figs. 1–4), we kept using the passive mode but added 
a delay (1 s or 1.5 s) between the sound cue and reward delivery. Given 
that mice started licking as soon as they entered the corridor and until 
they received the water, adding a delay versus active-reward mode did 
not change how the mice behaved (Figs. 1–4).
Behavioural training. All animals were handled via refined handling 
techniques for at least 3 days before being acclimated to head fixation 
on the ball. Animals were acclimated gradually (0.5–1 h per day) on the 
ball over at least 3 days until they could be head fixed without exhibiting 
any signs of distress. Then, animals began a running training regiment 
(1 h per day), which lasted for at least 5 days to ensure they could run 
smoothly and continuously on the ball before being exposed to the 


--- Page 10 ---
Article
closed-loop virtual linear corridor. For water-restricted mice, we trained 
them for 2 days to get used to acquiring water from the spout when no 
stimulus was presented, before the virtual reality + reward training ses-
sion. The VRn and VRg pretraining groups of mice (Fig. 5) were trained 
to acquire water from the spout on the last 2 days of unsupervised 
pretraining with no stimuli presented, after the virtual reality session 
ended to avoid the associative learning between stimuli and rewards. 
For the group without pretraining (Fig. 5), learning to get reward from 
the spout was similarly carried out after the running training session 
on the last 2 days of running training.
For the behaviour-only experiment, all animals started training in 
the virtual reality + reward training session on a Monday and continued 
training for exactly 5 days. The first day of training consisted of pas-
sive reward training, during which the reward was always delivered 
to the mouse in the rewarded corridor at the beginning of the reward 
zone. The next 4 days consisted of active reward training, during which 
the mice were required to lick in the reward zone to trigger the reward. 
This ensured a consistent training schedule during the critical learning 
period. The beginning of the reward zone was randomly chosen per 
trial from a uniform distribution between 2 m and 3 m, and continued 
until the end of the corridor. This meant that the earliest position in 
the rewarded corridor in which the mouse can receive the reward was 
a range of 2–3 m.
For imaging mice, the sound cue was presented in all trial types, for 
task and unsupervised mice, and the time of the sound cue was ran-
domly chosen per trial from a uniform distribution between positions 
0.5 m and 3.5 m. For task mice, the sound cue indicated the beginning 
of the reward zone in the rewarded corridor. The reward was delivered 
if a lick was detected after the sound cue in the rewarded corridor. As 
mice kept licking (anticipatory licking) as soon as they entered the 
reward corridors and learned to lick right after the sound cue, the 
reward delivery locations were also approximately uniformly distrib-
uted between 0.5 m and 3.5 m (Fig. 1c). In some mice, the reward was 
delivered passively with a delay after the sound cue, but these mice still 
showed anticipatory licking before the sound cue. To rule out whether 
the licking was due to detecting signals related to the reward delivery, 
such as water coming out the spout or sound produced by solenoid 
valve, we considered a lick response if the mouse licked at least once 
inside the corridor but before the sound cue. Although the rewards 
were absent, the sound cue was still presented in the unsupervised 
training experiment for consistency.
Data analysis
For analysis, we used Python 3 (ref. 59), primarily based on numpy and 
scikit-learn60,61, as well as Rastermap39. The figures were made using 
matplotlib and jupyter-notebook62,63.
Processing of calcium imaging data. Calcium imaging data were 
processed using Suite2p32, available on GitHub (www.github.com/
MouseLand/suite2p). Suite2p performs motion correction, region of 
interest detection, cell classification, neuropil correction and spike 
deconvolution as previously described64. For non-negative deconvo-
lution, we used a timescale of decay of 0.75 s (ref. 65). All our analyses 
were based on deconvolved fluorescence traces.
Neural selectivity (d′). To compute the selectivity index d′, illustrated 
in Fig. 1f, we only selected data points inside the 0–4-m region of the 
corridors where the textures were shown. We excluded the data points 
in which the animal was not running, so that all data points included 
for calculating the selectivity index came from similar engagement or 
arousal levels of the mice. Note that these data points are computed 
from original estimated deconvolved traces without interpolation. 
We first calculated the means (μ1 and μ2) and standard deviations 
(σ1 and σ2) of activities for any two corridors, then computed the d′. The 
criteria for selective neurons was d′ ≥0.3:

Retinotopy. Retinotopic maps for each imaging mouse were computed 
based on receptive field estimation using neural responses to natu-
ral images (at least 500 natural images repeated 3 times each). This 
proceeded in several steps:
(1) Obtained a well-fit convolutional encoding model of neural res­
ponses with an optimized set of 200 spatial kernels, using a refer-
ence mouse (Extended Data Fig. 1b).
(2) Fitted all neurons from our imaging mice to these kernels to identify 
the preferred kernel and the preferred spatial position (Extended 
Data Fig. 1c).
(3) Aligned the spatial position maps to a single map from the refer-
ence mouse.
(4) Outlined the brain regions in the reference mouse using spatial 
 maps and approximately following the retinotopic maps from 
ref. 33.
Compared with previous approaches, ours took advantage of single- 
neuron responses rather than averaging over entire local populations, 
and by using natural images that we can better drive neurons and obtain 
their specific receptive field models. The mapping procedure was 
sufficiently efficient that it could be performed in a new mouse with 
responses to only 500 test images each repeated 3 times. Below we 
describe each step in detail:
For step 1, using the reference mouse, we used the following to model 
the response of neuron n to image img:

algorithm was used to optimize the kernels, which alternated between: 
(1) finding the best position (xn, yn) for each neuron n, as well as the 
best kernel kn and the best amplitude an; and (2) optimizing K given a 
fixed assignment (xn, yn, kn, an) for each neuron n. The first part of the 
iteration was done in a brute force manner: responses of each kernel 
at each location for each image were obtained and correlated with 
the responses of each neuron. The highest correlated match for each 
neuron was then found and its corresponding (xn, yn, kn, an) was used 
to fit K. The best estimate for kernels K was approximately equivalent 
to averaging the linear receptive field all cells n assigned to a kernel 
kn after alignment to their individual spatial centres xn, yn. After each 
iteration, the kernels were translated so their centres of mass would 
be centred in the 13 × 13 pixel frame. The centre of mass was obtained 
after taking the absolute value of the kernel coefficients. After less than 
ten iterations, the kernels converged to a set of well-defined filters 
(Extended Data Fig. 1b).
For step 2, after the kernels K were estimated once, for a single- 
reference recording, we used them for all recordings by repeating 
the first step of the iterative algorithm in step 1 with a slight modifi­
cation. Instead of assigning each neuron (xn, yn, kn, an) independently, 
we averaged the 2D, maximum correlation maps of the nearest 50 neu-
rons to each neuron, and then took their maximum. This essentially 
smoothed the spatial correlations to ensure robust estimation even 
for neurons with relatively little signal (Extended Data Fig. 1c).
For step 3, to align spatial maps to the reference mouse, we used

Methods
All experimental procedures were conducted according to the Institu-
tional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC), and received ethical 
approval from the IACUC board at the HHMI Janelia Research Campus.
Experimental methods
Animals. We performed 89 recordings in 19 mice bred to express 
GCaMP6s in excitatory neurons: TetO-GCaMP6s × camK2a-tTa mice 
(available as RRID:IMSR_JAX:024742 and RRID:IMSR_JAX:003010)52. 
Of these mice, 13 were male and 6 were female, and ranged from 2 to 11 
months of age. Mice were housed in reverse light cycle, and were pair 
housed with their siblings before and after surgery. The mice had a run-
ning wheel in their cage, as well as corncob bedding with Nestlets. Dur-
ing training and imaging periods, we replaced the running wheel with 
a tube, to potentially motivate the mice to run longer while head fixed. 
Owing to the stability of the cranial window surgery, we often used the 
same mice for multiple experiments in the laboratory: two of the mice 
were used in ref. 53. Two of the mice were raised in complete darkness. 
We did not see differences compared with normal-reared mice, so we 
pooled them together. It was not possible to blind the experimenter 
with respect to behavioural experiments that involved water depri-
vation (see below). The number of mice in each experimental group 
was chosen to be comparable with other studies involving complex 
behaviour and imaging procedures such as ours. Mice were randomly

    26→We also used 23 C57 female mice for behaviour-only experiments. 
    27→These mice were only implanted with a headbar and not a cranial win-
    28→dow.
    29→Surgical procedures. Surgeries were performed in adult mice (post-
    30→natal day 35 (P35)–P333) following procedures previously described54. 
    31→In brief, mice were anaesthetized with isoflurane while a craniotomy 
    32→was performed. Marcaine (no more than 8 mg kg−1) was injected subcu-
    33→taneously beneath the incision area, and warmed fluids + 5% dextrose 
    34→and 0.1 mg kg−1 buprenorphine (systemic analgesic) were administered 
    35→subcutaneously along with 2 mg kg−1 dexamethasone via the intramus-
    36→cular route. For mice with cranial windows, measurements were taken to 
    37→determine bregma-lambda distance and the location of a 4-mm circular 
    38→window over the V1 cortex, as far lateral and caudal as possible without 
    39→compromising the stability of the implant. A 4 + 5-mm double window 
    40→was placed into the craniotomy so that the 4-mm window replaced the 
    41→previously removed bone piece and the 5-mm window lay over the 
    42→edge of the bone. After surgery, 5 mg kg−1 ketoprofen was administered 
    43→subcutaneously and the mice were allowed to recover on heat. The 
    44→mice were monitored for pain or distress, and 5 mg kg−1 ketoprofen 
    45→was administered for 2 days following surgery.
    46→Imaging acquisition. We used a custom-built two-photon mesoscope31 
    47→to record neural activity, and ScanImage55 for data acquisition. We used 
    48→a custom online z-correction module (now in ScanImage), to correct for 
    49→z and xy drift online during the recording. As previously described54, we 
    50→used an upgrade of the mesoscope that allowed us to approximately 
    51→double the number of recorded neurons using temporal multiplexing56.
    52→The mice were free to run on an air-floating ball. Mice were acclima-
    53→tized to running on the ball for several sessions before training and 
    54→imaging.
    55→Visual stimuli. We showed virtual reality corridors to the mice on three 
    56→perpendicular LED tablet screens, which surrounded each mouse 
    57→(covering 270° of their visual field of view). To present the stimuli, we 
    58→used PsychToolbox-3 in MATLAB57. The virtual reality corridors were 
    59→each 4 m long, with 2 m of grey space between corridors. The corridors 
    60→were shown in a random order. The mice moved forward in the virtual 
    61→reality corridors by running faster than a threshold of 6 cm s−1, but the 
    62→virtual corridors always moved at a constant speed (60 cm s−1) as long 
    63→as mice kept running faster than the threshold. Running was detected 
    64→using an optical tracking sensor placed close to the ball.
    65→The virtual reality corridors were created by concatenating four 
    66→random crops from one of four large texture images: circle, leaf, rock 
    67→and brick (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Grating stimuli (with angles of 0° 
    68→and 45°) were also used to create the virtual reality corridors for a subset 
    69→of mice (‘unsupervised gratings’ and VRg mice).
    70→For behaviour-only experiments, each mouse was trained with 
    71→rewards on one random pair of stimuli, such as leaf–circle or rock–brick. 
    72→Mice with unsupervised pretraining (VRn mice) were pretrained on the 
    73→same pair on which they were trained with rewards.
    74→For imaging experiments, mice from both the task and the unsuper-
    75→vised cohorts were only trained on or exposed to one pair of stimuli, 
    76→such as leaf–circle or rock–brick. For the mice exposed to the grating 
    77→stimuli, we presented more than one pair of naturalistic stimuli before 
    78→and after exposure to the gratings stimuli and recorded the neural 
    79→responses to the naturalistic stimuli pairs, so each mouse can have more 
    80→than one imaging session before and after. We also presented more than 
    81→one pair of naturalistic stimuli to the naive mice, so each naive mouse 
    82→can have more than one imaging session for testing naive responses.
    83→The two different types of leaf1-swap stimuli (Extended Data Figs. 6f 
    84→and 7a) were introduced separately for task mice but are pooled 
    85→together for statistics analysis. The two leaf1-swap stimuli were intro-

    87→treated as two different data points and pooled together for statistical 
    88→analyses.
    89→Water restriction procedure. Water restriction procedures were con-

    91→training condition, animals received an average of 1 ml water per day 
    92→(range of 0.8–1.2 ml depending on health status and behavioural per-
    93→formance). Before reaching 1 ml water per day after the initiation of

    95→from 2 ml per day to 1.5 ml per day until finally to 1 ml per day. The 
    96→behaviour-only mice were water restricted for 5 days right before 
    97→the virtual reality + reward training condition. Once the mice finished 
    98→the virtual reality + reward training session, the remaining water 
    99→(0.8–1.2 ml minus the amount received during experiment) was pro-

   103→Water reward delivery and lick detection. A capacitance detector

   108→get used to acquiring reward when stimuli were present. For all the
